modern_coref_001.text: Maria fixed the leaking pipe before the plumber arrived. She had noticed the leak the night before. The plumber thanked her for catching it early.

modern_coref_002.text: The manager reviewed Tom's proposal on Tuesday. He found two errors in the budget section. Tom corrected them before the next meeting.

modern_coref_003.text: The startup hired a new engineer named Priya. She had worked at a larger firm for six years. The founders were impressed by her portfolio.

modern_coref_004.text: The airline delayed the flight because of the storm. It finally departed three hours late. Passengers complained about the delay online.

modern_coref_005.text: Diego submitted the grant application last week. He had spent months preparing the budget. The committee will review his application in April.

modern_coref_006.text: The city council approved a new park downtown. It will open to the public next summer. Residents have already started planning events there.

modern_coref_007.text: Sam and his sister Lily opened a bakery together. He handles the finances while she bakes every morning. Customers say her sourdough is the best in town.

modern_coref_008.text: The pharmacy received a shipment of vaccines on Monday. It stored them in a refrigerated unit overnight. Nurses administered the vaccines the next morning.

modern_coref_009.text: Elena launched a podcast about local history. She interviews a new guest every week. Listeners praised her first episode online.

modern_coref_010.text: The technician installed a new router for the office. It doubled the wireless speed immediately. Employees noticed the improvement within a day.

g2_dense_boat_rose_boatman_edgar_thomas.text: "Sit still, children, do not move about in the boat," said Mr. Rose to the young folks he was taking for a trip on the water. There were in the boat Mr. Rose, the boatman, and several little boys and girls. "Keep still, please, young gentlemen," said the boatman, when Edgar Rose and Thomas Read began to move from one side to the other. They kept quiet for a short time only, and Edgar soon wanted a stick which Thomas held in his hand. He lost his balance in trying to get the stick, and fell into the water. Mr. Rose started up, and stretched out his arms to save him, but in so doing, they upset the boat.

g2_dense_bubble_harry_robert_willie.text: The boys have come out on the porch to blow bubbles. "Ha, ha!" laughs Robert, as a bubble comes down softly on the old cat's back, and does not burst. Willie tries to make his bubble do the same, and it comes down on the cat's face, and makes her sneeze. "She would rather wash her face without soap," says Harry. "Now let us see who can make the biggest bubble." "Mine is the biggest," says Robert. "See how high it floats in the air! It has burst." "I can see the house and the trees and the sky in mine," says Willie; "and such beautiful colors." "I know how many colors there are," says Harry. "Just as many as there are in the rainbow."

g2_dense_james_sport_dodger.text: James White has two dogs; one is a Newfoundland dog, and the other is a Scotch terrier. Sport is a good watchdog, and every night he guards the house while James and his father are asleep. In the daytime, James often uses Sport for his horse, and hitches Sport to a little wagon. The name of James's Scotch terrier is Dodger; he is called Dodger because he jumps about so friskily. Dodger has very bright eyes, and he does many funny things. The other day he took baby's red stocking, and had great fun with it, but he spoiled it in his play, and James had to scold him.

g2_dense_katie_mary_mother_fire.text: One winter night, Mrs. Lord and her two little girls sat by a bright fire in their pleasant home. At last, Katie finished her work, and, looking up, said, "Mother, I think the fire is brighter than usual." "And I was about to say," cried Mary, "that this is a better light than we had last night." "My dears," said their mother, "it must be that you feel happier than usual to-night." "But, mother," said Mary, "I do not see why we are happier now than we were then." "I know why!" said Katie. "It is because we have all been doing something useful to-night." "You are right, my dear," said their mother, "I am glad you have both learned that."

g2_dense_sam_harry_blindman.text: So Sam walked on, very sad. Soon after, a fine carriage came up, and in it were Harry and his mother. The blind man stood, and held out his hat. "Let us give the poor man something," said Harry to his mother. His mother gave him some cents, and Harry took them, but did not put them into the man's hat. He threw them into the hedge as far as he could, and the poor man could not find them, for he was blind. Sam had turned back to look at the fine carriage, and he saw Harry throw the cents into the hedge. So Sam came back at once, and looked for the money until he found it all for the blind man.

g2_dense_willie_bounce_brown_river_rescu.text: Willie had strolled with Bounce down to the river, which was not more than two blocks from his father's store. Bounce lay on the grass, watching the flies that buzzed around his nose. Willie jumped upon one of the logs floating near the shore, to see if he could throw a stone across the river. He drew back, and sent the stone with all his might; just as it left his hand, the log turned, and he fell into the water. Poor little Bounce gave a great yelp of distress, and ran up and down the bank, barking, looking first at Willie and then around. Then Bounce started, as fast as he could run, up the street to the store, and scratched against the door until Mr. Brown opened it. He caught hold of Mr. Brown's clothes, then ran to the door, then back again, catching at him, barking, and jumping. Brown thought of Willie, and as he came to the river, he saw Willie's hat floating on the water, and sprang in and caught him just in time.

g4_dense_fred_tom_katy_fire.text: Fred was wakened by the alarm and the red light streaming into his room, and hurried to the fire. "It is Mr. Barton's house, mother, do let me go," he said in eager, excited tones. Fred found Tom outside, in safety. "Where is Katy?" he asked. Tom, trembling with terror, said, "Katy is in the house!" "In what room?" asked Fred. "In that one," Tom answered, pointing to a window in the upper story. There was but one way to reach Katy, and Fred knew it, but he trusted in an arm stronger than his own.

g4_dense_george_jennie_two_mammas.text: "Mamma," said George West, as he came from school, "I can't help thinking about that poor little girl I told you of the other day." "Suppose you should carry her a handful of pretty flowers some time," said his mother. "Did you use to live in the country?" asked George. "Oh, yes," answered Jennie, "we used to live in a beautiful cottage." "Well, what made you move here?" "Papa died, and mamma was sick so long that the money was all gone," said Jennie. "Mamma," said George, that evening, "papa must give them some money, so they can go back to their home." "No," said his mother, "he can not do that, but perhaps he can help us contrive some way to assist them."

g4_dense_harry_frisk_annie.text: "Beg, Frisk, beg," said little Harry, as he sat on an inverted basket, eating a porringer of bread and milk. His little sister Annie, who had already dispatched her breakfast, sat on the ground opposite to him, twisting her flowers into garlands. "Beg, Frisk, beg!" repeated Harry, holding a bit of bread just out of the dog's reach, and the obedient Frisk squatted himself on his hind legs, waiting for Harry to give him the morsel. Frisk loved him dearly, much better than he did anyone else, because he recollected that Harry was his earliest and firmest friend. Harry took a fancy to him, and Harry's grandmother, who drove him off with a broom, at length let the little dog remain. He could fetch or carry either by land or water, and would pick up a ball of cotton if little Annie should happen to drop it, or take Harry's dinner to school for him.

g4_dense_john_sharp_ben_archery.text: "Come, come," said Master Sharp, "I am within one inch of the mark." John drew his bow, and shot, and the arrow struck within a quarter of an inch of Master Sharp's. "Shoot away," said Sharp, "but you must understand the rules; nobody is to borrow or lend." John seized his second arrow; "If I have any luck," said he; but just then the string broke, and the arrow fell from his hands. It was now Ben's turn to make his trial; his first arrow missed the mark, and the second was exactly as near as John's first. Master Sharp clapped his hands and danced for joy, but his dancing suddenly ceased, when careful Ben drew an excellent piece of cord from his pocket. "The everlasting whipcord, I declare!" cried John. "Yes," said Ben, "I put it in my pocket today because I thought I might want it."

g4_dense_lucy_john_aunt_kite.text: Lucy very kindly took up the kite and threw it into the air, but her brother neglecting to run off, the kite fell down again. Lucy once more took up the kite, but John was in too great a hurry; he ran off so suddenly that he twitched the kite out of her hand. "Well, who is to blame now?" asked Lucy. "Try again," said I. "There, there!" exclaimed John, "that comes of your throwing it all to one side." "As if I could make the wind blow straight," said Lucy. "O John, you should not have stopped," said I. "However, try again." "You may thank aunt for it, brother," said Lucy, "for you would have given it up long ago, if she had not persuaded you."

g4_dense_philip_stephen_robinson.text: "I will have revenge on him, that I will," said Philip to himself, with a countenance quite red with anger. "Who is that," said Stephen, "on whom you intend to be revenged?" "It was farmer Robinson's son who reduced it to this worthless state," replied Philip. Stephen coolly asked him what had induced young Robinson to break it. "He came up close to me, and began to call me names," replied Philip, "but I will make him repent of it." "To be sure," said Stephen, "he is a very wicked boy, and nobody likes him or will have anything to do with him." "All this is true," replied Philip, "but he has broken my cane, and I will be revenged."

g5_dense_hugh_agnes_mother.text: "Some things," replied his mother, "you can never play cricket, as every Crofton boy would like to do; you can never dance at your sister's Christmas parties." "O mamma!" cried Agnes, with tears in her eyes, thinking it cruel to talk so. "Go on!" cried Hugh, brightening. "You know what I feel, mother, and even sister Agnes sometimes makes out that it is no misfortune." "There will be little checks and mortifications continually, when you see little boys leaping over this, while you must stand out," said the mother. "O mamma!" exclaimed Agnes. "Well, and what else?" said Hugh.

g5_dense_michael_agnes_isabel_jacob.text: Michael and Agnes were childless, and Michael said to a man near him, "She has sunk into some mossy or miry place." A man came running toward the place where Michael and others were standing beside Agnes, who lay exhausted on the sward. Michael saw that he carried Lucy's bonnet, clothes, and plaid. Isabel took the clothes, and, narrowly inspecting them, said, "No, Lucy is yet among the living." Agnes had been able to walk home, and Michael and Isabel sat by her bedside. "I hear footsteps coming up the brae," said Agnes, and in a few moments the voice of Jacob Mayne was heard at the door. Michael stood up between Jacob and his wife, and looked into his heart.

g5_dense_squeers_mrssqueers_nicholas_smi.text: "Come," said Squeers, "let's go to the schoolroom, and lend me a hand with my school coat." Nicholas assisted his master to put on an old jacket, and Squeers, arming himself with his cane, led the way across the yard. "This is our shop, Nickleby," said the schoolmaster, as they stepped in together. "Now," said Squeers, giving the desk a great rap with his cane, "is that physicking over?" "Just over," said Mrs. Squeers, choking the last boy in her hurry, and tapping the crown of his head with the wooden spoon. Smike shuffled out with the basin, and Mrs. Squeers hurried out after him into the washhouse. "This is the first class in English spelling and philosophy, Nickleby," said Squeers, beckoning Nicholas to stand beside him.

g5_dense_tom_polly_madam_fan_maud.text: "Sing some more, dear," said Madam, in her gentle way, when Polly had done. "That's a jolly tune! Sing it again, please," cried Tom's voice, and there was Tom's red head bobbing up over the chair. "I can't sing any more; I'm tired," Polly said, and walked away to Madam, and the red head vanished. "You mus'n't mind my staring, dear," said Madam, "I haven't seen a little girl for so long." Polly asked, "Aren't Fan and Maud little girls, too?" "Oh, dear, no!" said Madam. "Fan has been a young lady this two years, and Maud is a spoiled baby." "That's the way I was brought up, and that's why Fan calls me old-fashioned," said Madam. "Tell more about your papa," said Polly.

g5v_flor_silin_wife.text: the famished inhabitants presented themselves before him, and begged for corn This good creature received them as brothers and, while his store remained, afforded all relief At length, his wife, seeing no end to the generosity of his noble spirit, reminded him how necessary it would be to think of their own wants and hold his lavish hand before it was too late said he

g5v_harry_gordon_master.text: The other boy was Harry Gordon though he was left in the room full twenty minutes, he never during that time stirred from his chair Harry had eyes in his head as well as the others but he had more integrity in his heart nor the key tempted him to rise from his feet he was engaged in the service of the old gentleman at Elm Tree Hall He followed his good old master to his grave, and received a large legacy for his upright conduct in his service

g5v_henry_wilkins_cherries.text: the old gentleman had placed a few artificial cherries at the top of the others, filled with Cayenne pepper one of these Henry had unfortunately taken and it made his month smart and burn most intolerably The old gentleman heard him coughing, and knew very well what was the matter The boy that would take what did not belong to him, if no more than a cherry, was not the boy for him Henry Wilkins was sent about his business without delay with his mouth almost as hot as if he had put a burning coal in to it

g5v_sherman_child_mother_bible.text: At length, he opened the Bible, and began to read. The child who was seated beside him made some little disturbance upon which Mr. Sherman paused and told it to be still Again he proceeded but again he paused to reprimand the little offender And this time he gently tapped its ear caught the attention of his aged mother, who now, with some effort, rose from the seat, and tottered across the room At length she reached the chair of Mr. Sherman she gave him a blow on the ear with all the force she could summon "you strike your child, and I will strike mine."

g5v_sherman_roguish_student.text: he was sitting and reading in his parlor A roguish student, in a room close by, held a looking-glass in such a position as to pour the reflected rays of the sun directly in Mr. Sherman's face He moved his chair, and the thing was repeated but the looking-glass still reflected the sun in his eyes He laid aside his book, went to the window many witnesses of the impudence expected to hear the ungentlemanly student severely reprimanded He raised the window gently, and then--shut the window blind!

g5v_tonish_colt.text: As to Tonish, who had marred the whole scene by his precipitancy he had been more successful than he deserved having managed to catch a beautiful cream-colored colt about seven months old that had not strength to keep up with its companions The mercurial little Frenchman was beside himself with exultation It was amusing to see him with his prize The colt would rear and kick, and struggle to get free when Tonish would take him about the neck, wrestle with him, jump on his back

g6_dense_joab_ahimaaz_cushi_absalom_king.text: A certain man saw it, and told Joab, and said, Behold, I saw Absalom hanged in an oak. Joab said unto the man, Why didst thou not smite him there to the ground? The man said unto Joab, I would not put forth my hand against the king's son. Then said Joab, I may not tarry thus with thee; and he took three darts, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom. Then said Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok, Let me now run, and bear the king tidings. And Joab said unto him, Thou shalt not bear tidings this day; then said Joab to Cushi, Go, tell the king what thou hast seen. And Ahimaaz said again to Joab, let me also run after Cushi; and Joab said, Wherefore wilt thou run, my son? Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi.

g6_dense_omar_ali_mansour_banian_cadi.text: "Have confidence in me a few moments," said Omar; "accept Ali's bargain; let me choose in your stead." "Here it is," said Ali; "it weighs twenty pounds. Choose what you will." The stranger, beside himself with joy, took three diamonds and forced them on Omar, who put them in his girdle, and seated himself by his father. "Well done," said Mansour; "but it is my turn now; mark me well, and profit by the lesson I shall give you." "What I desire," said Mansour, "is the casket with all its contents; this young man has promised to give me what I please." "It is mere child's play," answered Omar; "but since you desire it, my father, you shall lose your suit." "Illustrious cadi," said Omar, "this young man is ready to fulfill his engagement; this is what he offers Mansour." "No one," interrupted the cadi, "and I least of all; the necklace is worth a hundred thousand piasters, is it not, Mansour?"

g6v_beethoven_hugh.text: He was one of the greatest musical composers that ever lived His great, his sole delight was in music When all his time and all his mind were given to music, he suddenly became deaf, perfectly deaf so that he never more heard one single note from the loudest orchestra While crowds were moved and delighted with his compositions, it was all silence to him Hugh said nothing

g6v_rip_old_woman.text: an old woman, tottering out from among the crowd, put her hand to her brow peering under it in his face for a moment it is Rip Van Winkle! it is himself! Rip's story was soon told for the whole twenty years had been to him but as one night

He went off to the wars, too was a great militia general, and is now in Congress Rip's heart died away at hearing of these sad changes in his home and friends and finding himself thus alone in the world Every answer puzzled him, too and of matters which he could not understand He had no courage to ask after any more friends
